question: How can I cut back on salt in my regular meals?
ideal_answer:
The Dietary Guidelines point most adults toward less than 2,300 mg of sodium a day — about one teaspoon of salt total. Three moves that help at TAMU: rinse canned beans and vegetables before cooking (cuts about 40% of the sodium); ask for sauce or dressing on the side at restaurants and dining halls; and when comparing packaged labels, pick the one with 5% Daily Value or less for sodium. Herbs, lemon, salsa, and black pepper carry the flavor without the salt.
SOURCE: guideline_sodium

question: What's a healthy breakfast at the dining hall?
ideal_answer:
A solid breakfast combines a whole grain, a protein, and some fruit — all usually available in a dining hall. Easy builds: a bowl of oatmeal with fresh berries and a side of Greek yogurt; a veggie omelet with whole-wheat toast; or a yogurt parfait with granola and fruit. If you're grabbing and going, a banana and a hard-boiled egg (or a yogurt) still carries you.

question: How much fiber should I eat?
ideal_answer:
The FDA Daily Value for fiber is 28 grams a day, and most college-aged adults get about half that. Easy ways to close the gap: a cup of oats or 100% whole-wheat toast at breakfast (4–5 g each), a cup of beans or lentils with lunch or dinner (7–10 g), a piece of fruit for a snack (2–4 g), and vegetables at two of your meals. You hit 28 g faster than it sounds.

question: Is white rice bad?
ideal_answer:
White rice isn't bad — it's just a refined grain, so most of the fiber and B vitamins are stripped out. The habit worth building is making at least half of your grains whole, which the Dietary Guidelines recommend. In the dining hall, choose brown rice when it's offered; at the store, pick 100% whole-wheat bread, oats, or quinoa to balance out the white rice meals.

question: How do I read a sodium label?
ideal_answer:
On a Nutrition Facts label, scan the sodium line and the % Daily Value next to it. Rule of thumb: 5% DV or less per serving is low, 20% DV or more is high. Check the serving size first — a can of soup is often 2 or 3 servings, so the real sodium you'd eat is 2–3× the number shown. When comparing two products, the one with the lower sodium % DV per serving is the simpler pick.

question: What if my planned option isn't available?
ideal_answer:
If your plan's option isn't there, pick the closest thing on offer — a better choice still counts even when it's not the one you wrote down. Three usual swaps: no whole-grain option? Pick the dish with vegetables or beans. No fish entrée? Grab beans or a lean grilled option. No lower-sodium side? Add a piece of fruit or a side salad to balance a saltier main. Save the real plan for the next time it IS available.

question: How many cups of vegetables a day?
ideal_answer:
About 2½ cups of vegetables a day is a common target for college-aged adults — more if you're active. Frozen and canned count (rinse canned to cut sodium), so there's no requirement that they be fresh. In practice: a bowl of soup with vegetables counts, a cup of salad counts, and the vegetable side at dinner counts. Stacking two meals plus a snack usually gets you there.

question: What's the deal with added sugars?
ideal_answer:
The Dietary Guidelines put added sugars under about 50 g a day (10% of calories) for most adults — the FDA label shows this as 10% DV. A 12-oz can of regular soda has about 39 g, so one drink can use up most of a day's room. The biggest wins at your age: swap sweetened drinks for sparkling water or unsweetened iced tea most days, pick plain yogurt and add fruit yourself, and scan cereal labels for the ones with less than 10% DV added sugars.
SOURCE: guideline_added_sugars

question: How can I get more whole grains at the dining hall?
ideal_answer:
The Dietary Guidelines recommend making at least HALF of your grains whole. At the dining hall, swap white rice for brown rice at the entrée line, pick oatmeal over pastries at breakfast, and ask for 100% whole-wheat bread on sandwiches when it's offered. Even one swap a day shifts your week in that direction.

question: How do I eat better on a tight budget?
ideal_answer:
Budget staples that pack nutrition: dry or canned beans and lentils, eggs, frozen vegetables, oats, canned tuna, peanut butter, rice, bananas, and store-brand yogurt. Frozen and canned are as nutritious as fresh for most things and last way longer, so less waste. A bag of beans costs about a dollar and makes 6+ meals. Buy what you'll actually use that week — unused fresh produce is where most food money disappears.

question: Any ideas for easy snacks between classes?
ideal_answer:
The combo that holds you is a protein or healthy fat plus a complex carb. A few that travel well: a banana with peanut butter, a Greek yogurt with granola, string cheese and an apple, trail mix (nuts + raisins), hummus with carrot sticks, or a hard-boiled egg plus whole-wheat crackers. Keep a few shelf-stable ones in your bag so you don't end up grabbing something sugary from the vending machine.

question: Is olive oil healthy?
ideal_answer:
Olive oil is one of the healthier cooking fats — it's mostly unsaturated, which supports heart health. Using it in place of butter when you cook, or as a salad dressing, is one of the easier heart-healthy swaps. Keep a bottle around; even a tablespoon on roasted vegetables makes them way more satisfying.

question: What should I order at a fast food place?
ideal_answer:
The useful words on fast-food menus: grilled, roasted, baked, steamed. The ones to notice: crispy, fried, breaded, loaded, smothered. At a burger place, a grilled chicken sandwich plus a side salad with dressing on the side is almost always a stronger pick than fried + fries. At a Mexican place, a bowl with beans, grilled protein, and vegetables tends to be lower in sodium than a loaded burrito. Water or unsweetened tea instead of soda carries the whole meal.
